newsitem.title: USA: Calif. legislator targets teen body piercing.
newsitem.headline: Calif. legislator targets teen body piercing.

text.p: Prompted by an angry parent, a California legislator has introduced a bill to force body piercers to get parental consent before they perform piercing on minors, his aides said on Friday.
Body piercing is a growing fashion in California, especially among teenagers. Not only ear lobes, but lips, tongues, noses, abdomens, nipples and even genitals can be pierced and rings inserted.

George Runner, a Republican state Assembly member from southern California, introduced a bill this month that would make it illegal to perform body piercing on anyone under the age of 18 without the written consent of a parent or guardian.
"I just believe that before some stranger starts poking needles into your kid, you ought to know about it," Runner said in a statement.

"This is not only a parental rights concern, it's also a health issue. Without any law in place, kids could find themselves in a place surrounded by unsterilized needles and equipment and without the guiding voice of parents to assist them in making a decision," he said.
Runner said body piercing could often have severe health risks for teenagers whose bodies were still developing, according to his aides.

Current California law makes it illegal for anyone under the age of 18 to be given a tattoo, but there is no law against body piercing of minors. However, Runner's office noted that many responsible piercing studios already only performed piercing on minors with parental consent.

Runner introduced the bill in response to a complaint from a constituent. The woman told Runner her teenage daughter had had her bellybutton pierced without her knowledge after being dared to do so by friends, Runner's chief of staff Rick Van Nieuwburg said. The angry mother demanded to know whether there was a law to prevent this.
Runner's measure is expected to be discussed in the Assembly Public Safety Committee next month, Van Nieuwburg said, adding he believed the legislature would pass the bill.
